Training on Koh Samui centres on Muay Thai camps, which double as the island's best-equipped gyms. At Superpro Samui in the Bophut–Chaweng area a drop-in class costs 500 THB and an indoor gym session 400 THB, with gym-only memberships at 1,000 THB a week or 2,000 THB a month and full training memberships at 1,250–3,000 THB a week or 2,000–10,000 THB a month in 2026. Lamai Muay Thai Camp trains Monday to Saturday, 07:00–19:00. The island's big races are the Samui Half Marathon (21 June in 2026) and the Neon Run (30 May in 2026). Train early or late: daytime highs are 29–33 °C all year.

Muay Thai camps

Most visitors who come to Samui to train come for Muay Thai. Camps run two group sessions a day, usually one in the morning and one in the late afternoon, each about two hours: skipping and shadow boxing, pad rounds with a trainer, bag work, clinch and conditioning. Beginners are welcome in group classes, and two or three sessions in the first week is plenty while you get used to the heat. A private lesson costs about 1,000 THB an hour at Superpro, and all-in transformation packages with a room, meals and private sessions cost 25,000 THB for a week, 48,000 THB for two and 85,000 THB for four. Sunday is the usual rest day.

Our full guide covers beginners' advice, kit, a typical training week and where to watch fights six nights a week: Muay Thai on Koh Samui. To watch rather than train, see Muay Thai fight nights or book fight-night tickets in Chaweng from 1,500 THB (child 750 THB).

The DTV visa for Muay Thai

Thailand's Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) has a "soft power" track that covers Muay Thai courses: 5 years' validity, multiple entries and stays of up to 180 days per entry, with a 10,000 THB fee and proof of 500,000 THB in funds. From 31 August 2026 applicants also need a recent police clearance and must apply in the country where they live. Camps issue the enrolment letter. Details in our Thailand visa guide.

Most people training for a month rent a scooter or a room within walking distance of the gym; the walk is easier than it sounds before 08:00 and after 17:00.

Choosing a camp or gym

  • Try a single class first before paying for a week or month.
  • Trainer ratio: in pad rounds, count how many students each trainer is holding pads for.
  • Level mix: ask whether beginners and fighters train separately, and how sparring is managed.
  • Equipment and hygiene: clean mats, working fans, a cold shower and gloves you can borrow or buy.
  • Schedule: check session times against your plans, and whether Saturday and Sunday sessions run.
  • Insurance: make sure your travel insurance covers combat sports and sparring.

Gyms, functional fitness and BJJ

Samui's best-equipped gyms are attached to the fight camps, which is why fighters, expats and visitors all train in the same places. Superpro's indoor gym has its own drop-in (400 THB), weekly (1,000 THB) and monthly (2,000 THB) rates, separate from the class memberships, and it runs HYROX-style fitness sessions (private 1,500 THB), Brazilian jiu-jitsu (privates 1,500–2,000 THB; kids' BJJ 2,500 THB a month) and recovery sessions with ice baths (500 THB drop-in; breathwork and ice bath private 2,000 THB).

Resort gyms are usually for in-house guests only, though some wellness resorts sell day passes: in 2026 Kamalaya's day passes started at 1,800 THB++, with a Pilates reformer class option at 3,090 THB++. We could not confirm a CrossFit-affiliated box operating on Samui in late 2026, so if CrossFit specifically matters, check the official affiliate map before you travel; the functional-fitness classes at the fight camps are the closest equivalent.

Running routes

  • Beaches at low tide: Chaweng has about 7 km of sand and Lamai about 4 km; at low tide the firm, wet sand near the water is the best flat running on the island. Maenam is quieter still. Check the tide before you go.
  • Early-morning roads: the quieter lanes behind Maenam and Bophut and the Choeng Mon loop work before about 07:00. Avoid the ring road (Route 4169): traffic is heavy, verges are narrow and motorbikes overtake on both sides.
  • Hills: Samui's interior roads climb steeply, for example up to the Na Muang waterfalls or the viewpoints above Lamai. Watch out for dogs on rural lanes.
  • Trails: hiking trails to waterfalls and viewpoints make good trail runs in the dry season; see hiking on Koh Samui.

Run at dawn (from about 06:00) or after 17:30, carry water, and wear something bright on the roads.

Outdoor fitness on the water

  • Open-water swimming: Choeng Mon and Chaweng Noi are the calmest east-side bays from January to September. Avoid red-flag days and the October–December monsoon swell on the east coast, and don't swim alone or at dusk. See beach safety.
  • Kayak and paddleboard: kayaks rent at Coral Cove for about 300 THB an hour; calm mornings are best. See kayak and SUP on Koh Samui. On the Ang Thong speedboat tour (1,800 THB) you paddle along limestone cliffs; the park is closed from 1 November to 15 December and reopens on 16 December.
  • Snorkelling days: the Pig Island and Koh Tan speedboat (1,450 THB, every day of the year) is an active, easy half day.

Recovery

Hard training in the heat needs proper recovery. A one-hour Thai massage costs about 300–500 THB at a good shop and loosens tight hips and shoulders; tell the therapist which muscles are sore and ask for lighter pressure on bruises. Ice baths and breathwork sessions are available at some fight camps (Superpro's recovery drop-in is 500 THB), and a yin or restorative yoga class twice a week helps mobility. Sleep matters most: aim for 8 hours, with an afternoon rest between sessions.

Heat and hydration

Samui is hot and humid all year: highs of 29–33 °C, sea temperatures of 28–30 °C and little relief at night. Heat illness is the most common reason visitors stop training.

  • Build up over the first 3–5 days; your body needs about a week to acclimatise.
  • Train before 09:00 or after 16:30, and drink before you're thirsty.
  • Add electrolytes or oral rehydration salts (sold in every pharmacy and 7-Eleven) after long sessions.
  • Stop if you feel dizzy, stop sweating, get a headache or feel sick, and cool down in shade.
  • Cover grazes and blisters; skin wounds infect easily in the humidity.
  • Get travel insurance that covers combat sports if you plan to spar.

Hospitals and clinics, including sports injuries: hospitals on Koh Samui.
